calc_defs.name: MagnetCryogenicLoad
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Magnet Cryogenic Load

Calculates refrigeration power required for superconducting magnet systems.

Heat loads include:
1. Nuclear heating from neutron/gamma radiation
2. AC losses from field ramping (small for steady-state)
3. Structural heat leak from room-temperature supports

Refrigeration power scales as (T_ambient / T_operating) / carnot_efficiency
due to thermodynamic work required to pump heat from cryogenic to ambient.

Formula:
thermal_load = nuclear_heating + ac_losses + heat_leak
cooling_power = (thermal_load / operating_temp) × (300K / carnot_eff)

Source: PyFECONS thermal.py lines 18-64, cas220103_coils.py lines 230-250
Reference: ITER cryogenic system design
Typical Values:
- Nuclear heating: 0.05 × P_neutron × (A_magnet / A_total)
- Heat leak: 0.05 MW per m³ of magnet volume
- Carnot efficiency: 0.2-0.4 (realistic refrigerator)
Assumptions:
- 5% of neutron power reaches magnets (95% absorbed by blanket/shield)
- Steady-state operation (no transient field ramping)
- Uniform nuclear heating distribution
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: CoolantPumpPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Coolant Pump Power

Calculates mechanical pump power required for primary/secondary coolant loops.

Power required to circulate coolant at specified flow rate against system
pressure drop. Accounts for pump efficiency (mechanical + hydraulic losses).

Formula:
pump_power = (flow_rate × pressure_drop) / pump_efficiency

Alternate formulation from PyFECONS:
pump_power = f_pcppf × p_thermal_electric
where f_pcppf = primary coolant pumping power fraction (typically 0.06)

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py line 26
Reference: Fluid mechanics pump power equation
Typical Values:
- f_pcppf = 0.06 (6% of thermal electric power)
- Pump efficiency = 0.5-0.8
- Pressure drop = 0.5-2.0 MPa (depends on loop design)
Assumptions:
- Incompressible fluid
- Steady-state flow
- Single-speed pumps (no variable frequency drives)
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: HeatingWallPlugPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Heating Wall-Plug Power

Calculates total electrical power consumed by auxiliary heating systems
to deliver specified plasma heating power.

Heating systems (NBI, ECRH, ICRH) have efficiency losses:
- NBI: 30-50% (ion source, accelerator, neutralizer, duct transmission)
- ECRH: 40-60% (gyrotron efficiency, transmission, coupling)
- ICRH: 50-70% (RF amplifier efficiency, antenna coupling)

Formula:
wall_plug_power = delivered_power / heating_efficiency

Source: PyFECONS inputs.json lines 35-39
Reference: NBI system design (ITER, DEMO)
Typical Values:
- NBI efficiency: 0.3-0.5
- ECRH efficiency: 0.4-0.6
- ICRH efficiency: 0.5-0.7
Assumptions:
- All delivered power couples to plasma
- Steady-state operation
- No shine-through losses (neutral beams fully absorbed)
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: VacuumPumpPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Vacuum Pump Power

Calculates electrical power for mechanical vacuum pumps (roughing, turbo).
Does not include cryopump refrigeration (separate calculation).

Power scales with pumping speed and operating pressure. Practical vacuum
pumps have efficiency 30-50% due to motor and mechanical losses.

Formula:
pump_power_per_unit = (pumping_speed × pressure) / 1e6
pump_power = pump_power_per_unit × pump_count / efficiency

Source: PyFECONS cas220106_vacuum_system_costs.py
Reference: Vacuum technology fundamentals
Typical Values:
- Pumping speed: 200 m³/s total (48 pumps × 4.17 m³/s each)
- Base pressure: 1e-4 Pa (10⁻⁶ torr)
- Pump efficiency: 0.3-0.5
Assumptions:
- Constant pumping speed (actual speed varies with pressure)
- All pumps operating simultaneously
- No regeneration cycles
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: CryoPumpRefrigeration
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Cryopump Refrigeration Power

Calculates refrigeration power for cryogenic vacuum pumps.
Distinct from mechanical vacuum pumps - uses cryogenic surfaces to
condense/adsorb gas molecules.

Refrigeration power determined by:
1. Gas load (molecules condensing release heat of condensation)
2. Radiation heat load from warm surfaces
3. Conduction through supports
4. Carnot penalty (T_ambient / T_cryo)

Formula:
thermal_load = cryo_pump_count × pump_capacity × load_factor
refrigeration_power = thermal_load × (T_ambient / T_cryo) / carnot_eff

Source: PyFECONS inputs.json line 24
Reference: Cryopump design literature
Typical Values:
- Load factor: 0.001 MW per m³/s (empirical)
- Operating temp: 10-20K
- Carnot efficiency: 0.2-0.4
Assumptions:
- Continuous operation (no regeneration during pulse)
- Uniform gas load distribution
- Steady-state thermal loads
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: TritiumProcessingPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Tritium Processing Power

Calculates power for tritium fuel cycle systems:
- Isotope separation (cryogenic distillation)
- Tritium extraction from breeding blanket
- Purification and impurity removal
- Storage and delivery systems

Power scales with tritium throughput, which is proportional to fusion power.
Each D-T fusion reaction consumes 1 tritium nucleus, producing 17.58 MeV.

Formula:
tritium_burn_rate = fusion_power / 17.58  // MW → reactions/s
processing_power = tritium_burn_rate × processing_factor

Source: PyFECONS inputs.json line 29
Reference: ITER tritium systems design
Typical Values:
- Processing factor: empirical constant ~ 0.004 MW per MW fusion
- Expected for CATF: 10 MW (for 2600 MW fusion)
Assumptions:
- Processing power scales linearly with throughput
- Includes all tritium handling systems
- Steady-state fuel cycle (no startup inventory)
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: AuxiliarySystemsPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Auxiliary Systems Power

Calculates power for plant auxiliary systems:
- Building HVAC and lighting
- Diagnostics and instrumentation
- Control systems and computers
- Communication and security systems
- Maintenance equipment

Power estimated as fraction of gross electric output (empirical scaling).

Formula:
auxiliary_power = gross_electric × auxiliary_fraction

Source: PyFECONS inputs.json line 30 (p_house)
Reference: Power plant auxiliary load studies
Typical Values:
- Auxiliary fraction: 0.005-0.015 (0.5-1.5% of gross)
- Expected for CATF: ~10-14 MW (for ~1500 MW gross)
Assumptions:
- Auxiliary loads scale with plant size
- Includes all non-process loads
- Steady-state operation
Last Updated: 2025-11-09

calc_defs.name: ThermalCycleEfficiency
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Thermal Cycle Efficiency Calculation

Calculates the thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency for a heat engine
operating between hot (blanket outlet) and cold (heat rejection) temperatures.

The efficiency is limited by the Carnot efficiency (thermodynamic maximum)
and further reduced by real cycle losses (friction, heat transfer, turbine
efficiency, etc.).

Carnot Efficiency (ideal):
η_carnot = (T_hot - T_cold) / T_hot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot

Real Cycle Efficiency:
η_thermal = η_carnot × η_real

where η_real = 0.5-0.9 accounts for:
- Turbine isentropic efficiency (85-95%)
- Pump/compressor losses (80-90%)
- Heat exchanger effectiveness (90-98%)
- Pressure drops and piping losses
- Condenser/radiator losses

Typical Fusion Power Plant Thermal Cycles:

1. Water/Steam Rankine Cycle:
- T_hot: 550°C (823 K) - Limited by blanket materials
- T_cold: 30°C (303 K) - Cooling tower/water
- η_carnot: 63%
- η_real: 0.55-0.65
- η_thermal: 35-41%
- Status: Mature, widely used, reliable

2. Helium Brayton Cycle:
- T_hot: 700°C (973 K) - Helium-cooled blanket
- T_cold: 30°C (303 K)
- η_carnot: 69%
- η_real: 0.55-0.60
- η_thermal: 38-42%
- Status: Demonstrated in HTGR, good for fusion

3. Supercritical CO2 Brayton:
- T_hot: 650°C (923 K) - Advanced materials
- T_cold: 30°C (303 K)
- η_carnot: 67%
- η_real: 0.64-0.70
- η_thermal: 43-47%
- Status: Experimental, high potential

Temperature Constraints:
- T_hot limited by:
- First wall materials (tungsten, reduced activation steels)
- Blanket structural materials (EUROFER, V-alloys)
- Tritium permeation (higher T increases permeation)
- Typically <750°C for near-term materials
- T_cold limited by:
- Ambient conditions (air, water temperature)
- Cooling tower approach (5-15°C)
- Typically 20-40°C

Formula:
η_carnot = (T_hot - T_cold) / T_hot
η_thermal = η_carnot × η_real

Source: Web research on fusion thermal conversion (2024-2025)
Reference: DEMO power conversion system studies
Helium cooling for fusion blankets
Supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle research
Typical Values:
T_hot: 550-750°C (823-1023 K)
T_cold: 20-40°C (293-313 K)
η_real: 0.5-0.9
η_thermal: 0.35-0.47
Constraints:
- T_hot limited by materials (<750°C typically)
- T_cold limited by environment (20-40°C)
- η_real accounts for all real cycle losses
Assumptions:
- Steady-state operation
- No transient temperature variations
- Ideal heat rejection (environment acts as infinite sink)
Updates:
- 2025-12-08: Exposed eta_carnot as output for thermodynamic validation
and debugging. Enables verification of 2nd law (eta_thermal < eta_carnot)
Last Updated: 2025-12-08

calc_defs.name: ScientificQFactor
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Scientific Q Factor (Plasma Physics Performance)

Q_sci measures the plasma's ability to produce fusion power relative to
the external heating power required to sustain the plasma. It is the
fundamental metric of plasma confinement quality.

Performance levels:
- Q < 1: Sub-ignition (net energy sink in plasma)
- Q = 1: Break-even (fusion power equals input)
- Q = 5-10: High-gain (good confinement)
- Q > 20: Approaching ignition (self-sustaining)
- Q = ∞: Ignition (no external heating needed)

Formula:
Q_sci = P_fusion / P_input

ITER Target: Q_sci = 10
- 500 MW fusion power
- 50 MW heating power
- Demonstrates scientific feasibility of fusion energy

CATF MFE Baseline: Q_sci = 52
- 2600 MW fusion power
- 50 MW heating power
- Excellent plasma performance

Source: Standard fusion plasma physics definition
Reference: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py line 28
ITER Physics Basis (1999)
Assumptions:
- Steady-state operation
- All heating power couples to plasma
- No transient startup/shutdown effects
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

calc_defs.name: EngineeringQFactor
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Engineering Q Factor (System-Level Performance)

Q_eng measures the overall system's ability to produce gross electric power
relative to ALL auxiliary power consumption. Unlike Q_sci which only considers
plasma heating, Q_eng accounts for:
- Plasma heating systems
- Magnet cryogenics and power supplies
- Coolant pumps
- Vacuum systems
- Tritium processing
- All other auxiliary loads

Q_eng determines economic viability - the reactor must produce more electric
power than it consumes.

Performance levels:
- Q_eng < 1.0: Power sink (not viable)
- Q_eng = 1.0: Break-even (no net power)
- Q_eng = 1.1: Minimum viable (CATF target)
- Q_eng = 1.5: Good performance
- Q_eng = 5-10: Excellent (commercial target)

Recirculating Power Relationship:
f_recirc = 1 / Q_eng  (fraction of gross power consumed internally)
P_net = (1 - 1/Q_eng) × P_gross = (1 - f_recirc) × P_gross

Example (CATF target Q_eng = 1.1):
f_recirc = 1/1.1 = 0.909 = 91% recirculated
P_net = (1 - 0.909) × P_gross = 0.091 × P_gross = 9% to grid

Formula:
Q_eng = P_electric_gross / P_auxiliary_total

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 29-48
Reference: Fusion energy system engineering analysis
DEMO plant power balance studies
Typical Values:
CATF Target: Q_eng ≥ 1.1
Commercial Target: Q_eng = 1.2-2.0
Assumptions:
- All auxiliary power supplied from gross electric
- Steady-state operation
- No external grid power or energy storage
Updates:
- 2025-12-08: Exposed f_recirculating as output for economic validation
and reporting. Referenced in CATF design at designs/catf_mfe/physics.sysml:121
Last Updated: 2025-12-08

calc_defs.name: PlantEfficiency
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Plant Efficiency (Overall Energy Conversion)

η_plant measures the overall efficiency of converting fusion energy to
net electric power delivered to the grid. It accounts for:
- Thermal conversion efficiency (Carnot limit, cycle losses)
- Direct conversion efficiency (if any)
- All parasitic loads and auxiliary power

This is the key metric for comparing fusion to other energy sources.

Typical Plant Efficiencies:
- Fusion without direct conversion: 25-35%
- Fusion with direct conversion: 30-40%
- Best case fusion: 40-45%

Comparison to Other Technologies:
- Coal (subcritical): 33-37%
- Coal (supercritical): 37-40%
- Natural gas combined cycle: 50-60%
- Nuclear fission (PWR/BWR): 30-35%
- Solar PV: 15-20%
- Wind: 35-45% (capacity factor limited)

CATF MFE Target: η_plant ≈ 30-35%
- Competitive with fission
- Lower than gas, but carbon-free baseload

Formula:
η_plant = P_net / P_fusion

Source: Derived from PyFECONS power balance
Reference: Fusion power plant system studies
Energy technology comparison literature
Assumptions:
- All fusion energy thermalizes or converts directly
- No energy storage losses
- Steady-state operation
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

- Solar PV: 15-20%
- Wind: 35-45% (capacity factor limited)

CATF MFE Target: η_plant ≈ 30-35%
- Competitive with fission
- Lower than gas, but carbon-free baseload

Formula:
η_plant = P_net / P_fusion

Source: Derived from PyFECONS power balance
Reference: Fusion power plant system studies
Energy technology comparison literature
Assumptions:
- All fusion energy thermalizes or converts directly
- No energy storage losses
- Steady-state operation

calc_defs.name: PlasmaConfinement
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Plasma Confinement Calculation (ITER98y2 Scaling Law)

[PHASE 2 - INTERFACE PLACEHOLDER]

This calculation will implement the ITER98y2 energy confinement time scaling
law to predict plasma performance from machine parameters. In Phase 2, this
will replace the direct P_fusion input with a calculation based on:
- Plasma current and magnetic field
- Machine size (major radius)
- Plasma shape (elongation)
- Density and auxiliary heating power

ITER98y2 Energy Confinement Time Scaling Law:
τ_E = 0.0562 × M^0.19 × I_p^0.93 × R^1.97 × ε^0.58 × κ^0.78 × n_e^0.41 × B_t^0.15 × P_loss^(-0.69)

Where:
- τ_E: Energy confinement time [s]
- M: Average atomic mass [amu] (2.5 for DT)
- I_p: Plasma current [MA]
- R: Major radius [m]
- ε: Inverse aspect ratio (a/R) [dimensionless]
- κ: Plasma elongation [dimensionless]
- n_e: Line-averaged electron density [10^19 m^-3]
- B_t: Toroidal magnetic field on axis [T]
- P_loss: Loss power to plasma = P_fusion - P_alpha + P_aux [MW]

Validity Range:
- Aspect ratio: A = R/a = 2.5 - 5.0
- Plasma current: I_p = 0.8 - 24 MA
- Toroidal field: B_t = 1.0 - 6.0 T
- Major radius: R = 0.9 - 8.0 m

CATF MFE Concern:
- CATF has A ≈ 2.5 (borderline compact tokamak)
- At lower bound of validity range
- May need degradation factor or alternative scaling
- Compact tokamaks historically show reduced confinement

From τ_E, calculate fusion power using:
- Triple product: n × T × τ_E (Lawson criterion)
- Fusion reactivity: <σv>(T) for DT fuel
- Plasma volume and profile factors

Phase 1 Behavior (Current):
P_fusion = P_fusion_input (direct passthrough)

Phase 2 Behavior (Future):
1. Calculate τ_E from ITER98y2 scaling
2. Calculate aspect ratio A = R/a
3. Calculate plasma volume from R, a, κ
4. Calculate fusion power from n, T, τ_E, <σv>, volume
5. P_fusion = calculated value (not input)

Interface Design:
- Phase 1: All Phase 2 inputs present but not used
- Phase 1: P_fusion comes from p_fusion_input (direct)
- Phase 2: P_fusion calculated from plasma parameters
- No breaking changes when switching from Phase 1 to Phase 2

Source: ITER Physics Basis (1999), Nuclear Fusion 39(12), Equation 7
Reference: Web research on ITER98y2 scaling law (2025)
ITER confinement database analysis
Validity: A = 2.5-5.0, I_p = 0.8-24 MA
Concerns: CATF aspect ratio A ≈ 2.5 at lower bound
Status: INTERFACE ONLY - Implementation in Phase 2
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

calc_defs.name: TritiumBreedingRatio
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Tritium Breeding Ratio Calculation

[PHASE 2 - INTERFACE PLACEHOLDER]

This calculation will implement a simplified 1D neutronics model to estimate
tritium breeding ratio from blanket design parameters. TBR is critical for
fusion reactor fuel self-sufficiency - must be ≥ 1.05 to account for:
- Tritium decay (12.3 year half-life)
- Processing losses
- Startup inventory requirements
- Operational margin

Tritium Breeding Reactions:
Li-6 + n → T + He-4 + 4.8 MeV  (primary, all neutron energies)
Li-7 + n → T + He-4 + n - 2.5 MeV  (secondary, threshold E_n > 2.5 MeV)

Simplified 1D Beer-Lambert Neutronics Model:
Φ(x) = Φ_0 × exp(-Σ_t × x)

Where:
- Φ(x): Neutron flux at depth x [neutrons/cm²/s]
- Φ_0: Neutron flux at first wall
- Σ_t: Macroscopic total cross section [cm^-1]
- x: Depth into blanket [cm]

TBR Calculation Steps (Phase 2):
1. Calculate neutron flux profile through blanket
2. Account for neutron multiplication (beryllium, lead)
3. Calculate Li-6 breeding rate (fast + thermal neutrons)
4. Calculate Li-7 breeding rate (fast neutrons only, threshold reaction)
5. Apply geometric coverage factor (ports, penetrations reduce effective area)
6. TBR = (T atoms produced) / (fusion neutron)

Target TBR: ≥ 1.05 for self-sufficiency with margin
Typical Modern Designs: 1.12 - 1.15 with optimization

Key Parameters:
- Blanket thickness: 40-80 cm typical
- Li-6 enrichment: 30-90% (natural = 7.5%, higher = better TBR)
- Breeder material: Li, Li2O, Li4SiO4, LiPb eutectic, FLiBe
- Neutron multiplier: Beryllium (increases TBR by 10-20%)
- Blanket coverage: 70-85% (geometric, reduced by ports)

Phase 1 Behavior (Current):
TBR = tbr_assumed (typically 1.0, breed-to-burn assumption)

Phase 2 Behavior (Future):
1. Calculate neutron flux profile in blanket
2. Calculate breeding from Li-6 and Li-7 reactions
3. Apply neutron multiplication factor
4. Apply geometric coverage factor
5. TBR = calculated value (not input)

Simplified 1D Model Accuracy:
- ±10-20% compared to full 3D Monte Carlo (MCNP, Serpent)
- Sufficient for early design screening
- Phase 3: Integrate with full Monte Carlo for final design

Interface Design:
- Phase 1: All Phase 2 inputs present but not used
- Phase 1: TBR comes from tbr_assumed (direct)
- Phase 2: TBR calculated from blanket parameters
- No breaking changes when switching from Phase 1 to Phase 2

Source: Web research on tritium breeding (2024-2025)
Reference: DEMO blanket studies (HCPB, WCLL concepts)
Li-6/Li-7 nuclear data (ENDF/B-VIII)
Beryllium neutron multiplication
Target: TBR ≥ 1.05 (self-sufficient with margin)
Typical: TBR = 1.12-1.15 with optimization
Status: INTERFACE ONLY - Implementation in Phase 2
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

calc_defs.name: TorusMinorRadius
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Toroidal Minor Radius Calculation

Calculates the minor radius (a) of a toroidal annular layer from its
inner and outer radii relative to the major radius. The minor radius
represents the half-width of the layer cross-section at the midplane.

Formula: a = (r_inner + r_outer) / 2.0 - r_major

Where:
r_inner = inner radius of the annular layer [m]
r_outer = outer radius of the annular layer [m]
r_major = major radius (center of torus/plasma) [m]
a = minor radius (distance from major radius to layer center) [m]

Source: Standard tokamak geometry convention
Reference: Used in radial build volume calculations
Typical Values:
r_inner = 3.0-8.0 m (varies by layer, CATF MFE)
r_outer = 3.1-8.55 m (varies by layer, CATF MFE)
r_major = 3.0 m (CATF MFE)
a = 0.5-4.0 m (varies by layer)
Last Updated: 2025-12-22

calc_defs.name: TorusVolume
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Elongated Torus Volume Calculation

Calculates the volume of an elongated toroidal shell with elliptical
cross-section. Used for computing radial build layer volumes in tokamaks.

Formula: V = 2 * pi^2 * R * a^2 * kappa

Where:
R = major radius (center of torus) [m]
a = minor radius (half-width at midplane) [m]
kappa = elongation (vertical/horizontal aspect ratio)
V = volume [m^3]

Physical Basis: This is the volume of an elliptical torus. For a
circular torus (kappa=1), this reduces to V = 2*pi^2*R*a^2.

Note: Uses pi * pi as a static expression, which is valid per ADR-002
(true static expressions with only literals are allowed).

Source: Standard elliptical torus volume formula
Reference: PyFECONS radial_build.sysml lines 91-94
Typical Values:
R = 3.0 m (CATF MFE major radius)
a = 0.5-4.0 m (varies by layer)
kappa = 3.0 (CATF MFE elongation)
V = 50-2500 m^3 (varies by layer)
Last Updated: 2025-12-22
calc_expressions: volume = LiteralRationalEvaluation() * LiteralRationalEvaluation() * LiteralRationalEvaluation() * r_major * a * a * kappa

Documentation:

calc_defs.name: TorusSurfaceArea
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Elongated Torus Surface Area Calculation

Calculates the surface area of an elongated toroidal surface.
Used for first wall area and other plasma-facing surface estimates.

Formula: A = 2 * pi * R * a * kappa (simplified approximation)

Where:
R = major radius [m]
a = minor radius (or effective radius parameter) [m]
kappa = elongation
A = surface area [m^2]

Note: This is a simplified formula for the inner surface of a torus.
For a true elliptical torus, the exact formula involves elliptic integrals.
This approximation is consistent with PyFECONS usage.

Source: PyFECONS radial_build.sysml lines 449-452
Reference: Tokamak first wall surface area estimation
Typical Values:
R = 3.0 m (CATF MFE)
a = 0.5-2.0 m
kappa = 3.0 (CATF MFE)
A = 30-100 m^2
Last Updated: 2025-12-22
calc_expressions: area = LiteralRationalEvaluation() * LiteralRationalEvaluation() * r_major * a * kappa

calc_defs.name: MagnetSurfaceArea
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Magnet Surface Area Calculation

Calculates exposed surface area of magnet coils for nuclear heating
and cryogenic load estimates. Uses a fraction factor to account for
the portion of magnet surface exposed to radiation.

Formula: A = 2 * pi * r_inner * thickness * kappa * f_exposed

Where:
r_inner = inner radius of magnet layer [m]
thickness = radial thickness of magnet layer [m]
kappa = elongation
f_exposed = fraction of surface exposed (default 0.5)
A = exposed surface area [m^2]

Source: PyFECONS radial_build.sysml lines 455-457
Reference: Magnet nuclear heating surface area estimation
Typical Values:
r_inner = 6.5 m (CATF MFE TF coil inner radius)
thickness = 0.25 m (CATF MFE TF coil thickness)
kappa = 3.0 (CATF MFE)
f_exposed = 0.5 (half of surface faces inward)
Last Updated: 2025-12-22
calc_expressions: area = LiteralRationalEvaluation() * LiteralRationalEvaluation() * r_inner * thickness * kappa * f_exposed

calc_defs.name: AlphaNeutronSplit
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Alpha-Neutron Power Split from DT Fusion

In deuterium-tritium fusion, each reaction releases 17.58 MeV total energy:
- Alpha particle (He-4): 3.52 MeV (20.0%)
- Neutron: 14.06 MeV (80.0%)

The alpha particle is charged and deposits energy in the plasma (self-heating),
while the neutron is neutral and deposits energy in the blanket/first wall.

Formula:
P_alpha = P_fusion × (3.52 / 17.58) = P_fusion × 0.200227
P_neutron = P_fusion × (14.06 / 17.58) = P_fusion × 0.799773

Source: Nuclear reaction kinematics (D + T → He-4 + n)
Reference: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 94-105
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deuterium-tritium_fusion
Assumptions:
- 50-50 D-T fuel mix
- Complete fusion reaction (no partially burned fuel)
- Standard DT reaction energetics
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

calc_defs.name: BlanketThermalPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Blanket Thermal Power with Neutron Multiplication

Calculates total thermal power deposited in the blanket from:
1. Neutron energy deposition with breeding multiplication (M_n × P_neutron)
2. Auxiliary input power thermalized (P_input)
3. Recovered waste heat from pumping and subsystems

Neutron multiplication (M_n = 1.1-1.3) comes from:
- Tritium breeding reactions (Li-6 + n → T + α + 4.8 MeV)
- Beryllium neutron multiplication (Be-9 + n → 2n + ...)
- Additional exothermic nuclear reactions in blanket materials

Waste heat recovery accounts for:
- Coolant pumping inefficiency (f_pump × η_pump)
- Subsystem waste heat (f_subsystem)
Both scale with thermal power available for conversion

Formula:
P_thermal = (M_n × P_neutron) + P_input +
η_thermal × (f_pump × η_pump + f_subsystem) × (M_n × P_neutron)

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 15-21
Reference: DEMO blanket studies, ITER blanket design documentation
Typical Values:
M_n = 1.1-1.3 (neutron energy multiplication)
f_pump = 0.06 (6% pumping power fraction)
η_pump = 0.5 (50% pumping efficiency)
f_subsystem = 0.03 (3% subsystem power fraction)
Assumptions:
- Uniform blanket energy deposition
- All auxiliary power thermalizes in blanket
- Pump and subsystem waste heat is recoverable
Last Updated: 2025-11-03
calc_expressions: p_thermal = m_neutron * p_neutron + p_input + eta_thermal * f_pump * eta_pump + f_subsystem * m_neutron * p_neutron

calc_defs.name: GrossElectricPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Gross Electric Power from Thermal and Direct Conversion

Converts thermal energy to electricity through two parallel paths:
1. Thermal conversion (blanket → steam/gas → turbine → electricity)
2. Direct conversion (alpha particles → electricity, experimental)

Thermal Conversion (η_thermal = 0.35-0.47):
- Limited by Carnot efficiency: η_carnot = 1 - T_cold/T_hot
- Material temperature limits (blanket outlet ~550-750°C)
- Real cycle losses reduce Carnot efficiency by 10-20%
- Water/steam Rankine: 35-41%
- Helium Brayton: 38-42%
- Supercritical CO2: 43-47%

Direct Conversion (η_direct = 0.0 or 0.5-0.85):
- Phase 1 baseline: η_direct = 0.0 (all alpha thermalizes)
- Future: Magnetic expansion or traveling wave direct converter
- Experimental technology, not mature

Formula:
P_electric_gross = η_thermal × P_thermal + η_direct × P_alpha

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 22-27
Reference: Rankine/Brayton cycle thermodynamics
DEMO power conversion system design
Direct conversion experimental results
Typical Values:
η_thermal = 0.35-0.47 (thermal cycle efficiency)
η_direct = 0.0 (Phase 1) or 0.5-0.85 (future)
Assumptions:
- Phase 1: All alpha energy thermalizes (η_direct = 0)
- Material temperature limits constrain thermal cycle
- Thermal efficiency ≈ 0.8-0.9 × Carnot efficiency
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

- Phase 1 baseline: η_direct = 0.0 (all alpha thermalizes)
- Future: Magnetic expansion or traveling wave direct converter
- Experimental technology, not mature

Formula:
P_electric_gross = η_thermal × P_thermal + η_direct × P_alpha

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 22-27
Reference: Rankine/Brayton cycle thermodynamics
DEMO power conversion system design
Direct conversion experimental results
Typical Values:
η_thermal = 0.35-0.47 (thermal cycle efficiency)
η_direct = 0.0 (Phase 1) or 0.5-0.85 (future)
Assumptions:
- Phase 1: All alpha energy thermalizes (η_direct = 0)
- Material temperature limits constrain thermal cycle
- Thermal efficiency ≈ 0.8-0.9 × Carnot efficiency
Last Updated: 2025-11-03

calc_defs.name: NetElectricPower
calc_defs.doc_comment:
Net Electric Power after Parasitic Loads

Subtracts all auxiliary power consumption from gross electric output to
calculate net power delivered to the grid. Parasitic loads include:

1. P_coils: Magnet system power (superconducting coil cryogenics, resistive losses)
2. P_heating: Plasma heating systems (NBI, ECRH, ICRH - wall-plug power)
3. P_pumps: Coolant circulation pumps (primary, secondary loops)
4. P_cryo: Cryogenic refrigeration (magnet cooling, fuel systems)
5. P_vacuum: Vacuum pumping (torus, divertor, roughing pumps)
6. P_tritium: Tritium processing and fuel cycle (separation, purification)
7. P_auxiliary: Other auxiliary systems (control, diagnostics, building services)

Typical parasitic power fraction: 10-30% of gross electric
- Q_eng = 1.1: ~91% parasitics (CATF minimum viable)
- Q_eng = 1.5: ~67% parasitics (good)
- Q_eng = 5-10: ~10-20% parasitics (excellent)

Formula:
P_parasitic_total = P_coils + P_heating + P_pumps + P_cryo + P_vacuum + P_tritium + P_auxiliary
P_net = P_electric_gross - P_parasitic_total

Source: PyFECONS PowerBalance.py lines 29-48
Reference: ITER auxiliary power estimates
DEMO plant power balance studies
Typical Parasitic Fraction: 10-30% of P_gross (Q_eng = 1.1 to 10)
Assumptions:
- All parasitics supplied from gross electric output
- Steady-state operation (no transient startup power)
- No external grid power or energy storage
Updates:
- 2025-12-08: Exposed p_parasitic_total as output for Q_eng calculation
and power balance validation. See Issue C in research doc:
project/research/20251208-152235_codegen-pipeline-test-failures.md
Last Updated: 2025-12-08
